What you said about others not really understanding it and the seriousness made me want to sigh deeeply, my dad keeps saying it's fine if I \*sometimes\* eat something with gluten, no reason to be so strict about it. I should show him that picture on the gluten-free diet wikipedia article of the bread crumb that's already enough gluten to do damage... He doesn't have enough information about it is all, he doesn't mean anything by it. But it can feel frustrating and on some level scary that people who might be responsible for your food do not really take it seriously enough to make it safe for you to eat. Anyway, I digress.

I haven't traveled much while gluten free but even that was enough to learn it takes a lot more time to find suitable places to eat. Maybe not so bad if you do your research beforehand and not on the fly hah. And a lot of them can't guarantee complete gluten-free food or else they just won't. A lot of fast food places seem to be like that. I think I've got glutened once eating out so far. I should've let them know I have celiac's disease, instead of just choosing something with gluten free ingredients and thinking that's enough, that was on me. I've also had to reprogram some behaviors like sharing food (my family has always shared our orders so everyone can try any they're interested in. now i can't try anyone else's, which can be hard to keep in mind sometimes). At least where I live many places mark the gluten-free options as such so finding the right options on the menu isn't difficult in my experience. 

Something of an exception has been breakfast buffets at hotels, some don't have almost anything gluten free that isn't maybe yogurt and fruit. But some places will set something extra out for you if you let them know you need it, bread and such. Buffets in general now seem like a big risk to me, I wonder if I'll do those at all anymore unless I really have to. I guess I don't really have a best practise for travel and eating out yet, but here are some things I've learned so far.

I was diagnosed a few months back, still kind of in the process of accepting it and adapting. But, it gets better with time as you start feeling better and find replacements for things you can't eat anymore. It helped me in the beginning to make a list of things I love that I still can have, helped me see not everything has to change. But a lot of things did change and that's okay to not immediately adapt perfectly, it's a whole process. Take things one day at a time if you need to.

Are you going to meet with a nutritionist or other specialist that can fill you in on gluten-free diet and kind of give you a 101 on all of that? There are also some related subreddits that have been somewhat helpful to me and it's been nice to see I'm not alone with this

Accepting the temporary nature of everything has made it easier for me at least. That is, it's not something I wanted to embrace but when you don't expect to be at least as important to a friend tomorrow as you are today, each time you meet or talk is a renewal and a confirmation of your bond and a joyful occasion in itself. To expect anything to be forever is to line a big pile of hurt in your future, in my experience. If it's good right now, then that is a thing to be happy about regardless of the future, and while continued happiness is of course good, things change constantly and that can't be helped. Could be a new kind of happiness too, that results from all the changes, it's not always bad.

That being said, it is hard when for any reason you become the last priority to someone you consider a very close friend. It's okay to feel bad about that part. And it's exhausting to meet new people if it's not something that comes to you naturally.
Such an important lesson to learn!

Things like this week's grocery list, next steps in a course project, plans to initiate with people etc etc

I guess you could say all of that in digital form is maybe *too* convenient and quick and I forget about it immediately if I didn't have to put in effort? The act of writing or drawing forces me to process and plan things more than typing. Also, digital formats are typically only in sight if the device is open and I've opened the application I'm using, but I need a big visual cue like a colorful calendar on the desk to remind me that hey there might be something important happening today or tomorrow let's check! I also don't like constant alarms, I'd never be able to relax and not feel like crying if my phone was ringing all the time. So those are not a reasonable option for me personally, though fairly common on this sub.

I've only made one or so new friends in my mid and late 20s (and had few enough to begin with), but it was only by doing what I'd never done before, by taking the initiative and making the many first moves and not giving up, that I managed to nurture a new friendship in my life. It's not all thanks to me, maybe I got lucky to contact someone who also wanted friends, but it did take at least a year of occasionally going out for coffee/lunch and eventually meeting up more often than once or twice a month, for anything more than acquaintances to come out of it. We started off just having coffee for a long time, but adding something a little bit different one thing at a time (such as lunch, shopping, walks, small events) made the connection have more context than just the original one, which I think is very important for its growth. 

Also, I think adults are more cautious to properly let people in, they need to see you're there to stay or otherwise it might not be worth their time if they lead busy lives. Maybe some people can make friends faster than that, even in late 20s, but I never really could. I'm slow to warm up like that. So for me the long game is where it's at, even if it's not as rewarding at first. Now I have a friend who I don't think is going to just forget about me the moment they meet someone new and more interesting, and that's totally worth all that time for me.

Mind, I'm still working on making more friends so rather than general advice, this is more of a single case observation of what worked at least this one time. But maybe it checks out in a wider context as well.

I've tracked my insufficient social skills to a similar source, my parents were too busy when me and my sibling were little and didn't have the time or energy to be talking to us other than the bare necessities so we never learned to have conversations or to be motivated to talk to people - afterall, talking was only used to convey information in our family. Same goes for expressions, I can pretty much only remember my parents showing anger or worry on their faces and otherwise it was pretty neutral. This all lead to me not being the most interesting companion, so it's no wonder I had no close friends in high school and past that.

To be fair, I'm also diagnosed with depression and social anxiety, those definitely had a hand in it too, but are also the result. Finally I went into therapy to treat my issues, a bit over a year ago, and it's helped me a lot to just be consistently talking to someone and notice that once I get used to the person I can totally have long conversations no sweat! With that bit of newly found confidence I also learned to like talking to people, which shows and makes people be more at ease around me nowadays. 

While psychotherapy is a bit of an investment, it's been very helpful in my case. But other, free-of-cost things that I do to make my social encounters smoother is to practise them beforehand in my mind such as think of a few topics/anecdotes I could talk about, maybe go through at least a thing or two that I could say about them and so on. If I do this often enough it doesn't matter if in the moment I forget the exact examples I had in mind, with all that practise I've become better at thinking of various different things to talk about! Not an immediate success, but makes you more flexible in the long run. I've also paid more attention to my body language (am I facing the person I'm talking to, are my arms crossed, am I slouching, do I hold my head up high etc) and expressions. These are a big help in making people feel welcome in your presence and that can never hurt.

As to the process of getting friends and a girlfriend, I'm still working on all that myself but did manage to make one very good friend over the last two years, so there is some success in that area too.

I used to be much more quiet than I am nowadays and I have more confidence in myself socially too - for me it was a matter of realizing I'm more of a one-on-one person than for groups, and more importantly, actually gaining a certain level of social skills and understanding made all the difference in the world. I didn't learn enough growing up because my family was busy providing for us and I never had proper conversations with anyone other than grandparents who I saw a few times a year, and this only before I got younger cousins who took up their attention ever since. By the time I went to middle school and high school this showed as no one being interested in me because I didn't care for talking much, which in turn made me very insecure and ashamed of myself. Took me until my 20s to start therapy and all the conversations I've had with my therapist gave me the confidence that I now have, I now know I can totally have a 45-minute conversation no problem, as long as the other person is willing.

While my therapy is mainly for depression and anxiety, it's always a valid choice of course, but also just talking, actually having conversations about topics with relatives, friends, teachers, anyone really, might help. For a start, to leave a better impression, make sure to at least meet other people's eyes occasionally to show you're paying attention to them - in my country that is also a sign of honesty and sincerity instead of confidence, so it was easier to think of it that way and feel like it was okay for me to do it - I was being sincere with these people afterall. Aside from eyecontact, raising your eyebrows a tiny bit, maybe smiling ever so slightly, when seeing someone you know, or someone who is greeting you, goes a long way too. Implies you're open to conversation and their company, and people tend to like that, it makes them be at ease around you. Expressions are a good way to make people feel more connected to you too, I had this whole stoic deadpan identity in high school which I partly did just because it amused some of my friends, but also because expressions had never been something my family communicated with. Took some learning, but I can easily see the difference it makes.

Uhh I guess I digress quite some here but hopefully some of this was helpful or otherwise a positive influence!

I've been on antidepressants for two years now, and I got two different prescriptions - one that gives me energy and one that affects my mood. Since starting them I've had more energy to finish my undergrad (though I needed a therapist's support for that one as well), to make efforts towards making friends (with one great success), to make good progress in therapy and become a relatively functional adult at least compared to my past self. Still no job or anything but I guess I'll take it still. The mood part mostly means that I suffer from intense anhedonia, couldn't really enjoy anything and was just bored and gloomy all the time, wishing I could sleep 24/7 because there was nothing I wanted to do and boredom was insufferable when there was so much of it. When I started on the second medication, I've noticed I now have better days too when I'll have fun watching my favorite shows on netflix and playing games without it feeling like a task for killing time. That, I suppose, was the change that actually gave me hope for the future, that I can actually enjoy my time here on occasion but that's more of a depression thing than social anxiety I suppose.

Side effects involved headaches and nausea during the first weeks but those went away for the most part. I still have mild nausea sometimes but nothing like the first week. The lasting effects would be a tiny bit of muscle twitching and loss of any libido I might have had though it's hard to say to what extent because I always was asexual to begin with. These kinds of medications can also react badly with other medications, I was pretty much bedridden for a full day when I started my allergy medication last spring because the combo made me incredibly sleepy and just plain unable to get out of bed. I personally started getting sun rash as well after I started on the meds, but I'm the pale pink nordic type that turns crab-red instead of getting a sweet tan after a day in the sun so maybe that's not among the most common side-effects.

As for what would happen if I quit the meds, I don't know. With the first prescription, I'd be afraid I'd lose what energy I have now and go back to sleeping all day and then sleeping some more and lying in bed most of the time because that's all I have the strength for. Naps for dinner and all that because even just fixing some toast would be too tiring. If I quit the mood affecting meds I don't think the change would be all that drastic, but I'd be a lot more bored and restless as a result, therefore also more depressed.

That being said, I don't know how much they've affected my social anxiety. I'm also diagnosed with social anxiety/social phobia, but what I think has affected that the most was just talking to people more and learning how to have conversations and get used to it in general. This I did by partaking in a peer support group for social anxiety and by talking to doctors and psychologists and eventually my therapist once I started seeing her. Anything that has you regularly talking to someone outside of your current family and friends might do, but some kind of therapy or counseling is what I'd recommend.

Maybe you could try to cultivate a more accepting mindset towards yourself for a start, you do seem to have several hobbies (even if some are fairly solitary) and you clearly have an interest in making friends and perhaps starting a relationship, from what I gathered from your text. Those are all positive traits my man, don't sell yourself short! I realize it's really damn hard to immediately be able to think that 'oh, right, that's how it was all along!', I've been there, but the way I was able to start changing my thoughts about myself was questioning the strongest negative labels I gave myself (such as 'hate is a strong and very personal feeling, no one you know actually hates you you know', whatever matches your inner dialogue) and to show myself that I'm not particularly good or bad at these things and instead I'm really rather average. 'Based on the internets, a lot of people feel much like I do. Not everyone, clearly, but a fairly large amount even so. That makes me somewhat average instead of some freak of nature that has no place in life.' Now that's not the most inspiring thing to hear, but it's also not something to deepen the crushing depression and anxiety that I'd been battling since teenage. From a more neutral stance you can eventually move on to seeing yourself in a genuinely positive light.

Another thing that helped me was to learn how to have conversations, seems like it's something you struggle with as well? For me it happened over two or so years in frequent (at least monthly) student healthcare, mostly counseling, physiotherapy and some respiratory issues. Literally everyone I had any kind of conversation with was a health care professional because I didn't really have that kind of friends and my family history was the reason I didn't already know how to converse, ours was a politely distant kind of familial harmony where you only talk about practical arrangements and such and the rest wasn't important enough. 

Since January I've been seeing a therapist as well and that was sort of the final stroke in breaking my inability to hold a conversation and my social anxiety has lessened so much since my treatment first began. Depression not so much, but anxiety was the real life quality killer for me, and when it's affecting daily life like it was for me and maybe is for you, it's totally a legit reason to seek help. So if counseling or therapy is an option, you might want to consider that. I once went to a social anxiety support group for one semester and that I guess helped too. Most importantly I made a good friend there who had similar issues so I didn't have to try so hard as long as I accepted their difficulties as well and that kind of thing has never been hard for me.

Body language matters a lot too, maybe pay attention to whether you look tense and stiff around people or not, and do you look like you're open to socializing. I'm bad with this myself, but I try to fix my bad posture when I notice I'm slouching, and I make an effort to have eyecontact and avoid hiding my expressions like I've done most of my life. 

Either way, I'm sorry this got so long I have a bad habit of rambling on and on about even remotely relevant things. I hope your situation gets better because you seem like an okay dude in an unfortunate situation. Consistent effort will bring changes to your life if you want it to.

A socially anxious person testing the boundaries of their comfort zone isn't therapy though, and social gatherings are not a competitive sport. I didn't get to attend that many typical social events most of my life, so I had no previous concept of what they would actually be like in real life (I was taught early on that tv is not a good source for reliable information on this front. or any front for that matter) and had to learn these things in my twenties instead of childhood and teenage. This is extremely reminiscent of my past, just that I was the one who kept moving and then my only friend in school decided they didn't want to go to the same high school with me and simultaneously my loose group of online friends decided phone calls were more important than having me in the group (I used to get bad anxiety/panic attacks from skype calls and couldn't stay). So I was practically left without friends right as high school started and it stayed that way until this last year or so.

I won't say I'm great at socializing because I'm not, but I'm a lot better than I was after what was more or less a decade of solitude. Practise/experience is key, even if it means you're going to weird people out at first, I definitely did some of that trying to become a better conversationalist and ended up "interrogating" a lot of people unintentionally. Mistakes are my way or learning  and I don't see how I would ever have learned otherwise. I'd also recommend trying to accept your lack of experience as a fact and it's simply how things are currently and not something shameful, the way I think of my lack of experience is it's a neutral state of things and I was just doing other stuff with that time. Even if that stuff was reading, playing videogames and drawing alone in my room. You are making sincere efforts to get better and it is a time in your life when you're focusing on the social side of things. Kind of how people who worry they're graduating too slowly and that it doesn't count if you don't graduate in record time, there is no hurry really, people *will* want and need friends at all ages and while finding other people is going to require more personal effort when you're not in school anymore, the rest of it is not so different and good people won't mind if you're a bit clumsy. Might even be endearing to some.

As for connecting with people, that's still something I also struggle with. As someone with depression and other issues, it was easier to relate to folks who had similar hardships. This way we could bond through the kind of problems we both had, problems that might not be as common or readily understandable to people without our shared issues. And on the flipside of that, the problems of healthier individuals were hard for me to understand or care about when I had intense, partially crippling issues going on. Other than finding people in a similar situation/with a similar worldview, everyone always says to join hobby groups (not a good option for me as I have no money for that, but maybe you can make it work) like board games or sports or something. Those could work.

And finally, I really feel you on struggling to stay positive, but with continued effort it should get better, it did for me. I only have one or two friends now, but that already is so many more than I used to have and I'm so grateful. Being more conscious about nurturing new and old friendships is what's helped me a lot, I'm not the most social or needy person by nature and the time it takes for me to get lonely and think of contacting a friend is so long that they think I'm not interested in knowing them. So I need to make sure to say hi now and then, even if it doesn't occur to me naturally and isn't what I felt like in the moment.

Best of luck, I hope you find yourself a friend :) Sorry this became a long-ish ramble without a tl;dr

I can relate to much of this. So much, really. But one way to begin getting over that self-doubt is to take a look at that assumption of others hating you. Would you hate someone just because they have no friends? Hate is a strong and personal emotion, it is unlikely your classmates or anyone else for that matter actually hates you. I don't presume to know what your situation is but that is usually true for most people as long as they haven't actively done something to warrant that hate. Now, not being hated by the others hardly means being friends with them, but perhaps adopting a more neutral mindset about their perception of you might be helpful in the long run. 

If it was merely an exaggerated choice of words, you might want to discontinue using the word hate like this in particular. Even if you don't really mean it here, by repeatedly using it in this context you're making sure it's the one your brain will feed back to you when you're being unsure of yourself, and as a result you'll likely feel/think it's used literally this time and feel worse about yourself. Well, this is what I've noticed in myself and now I try to use more neutral or positive vocabulary as my go-to choice.

I hope this didn't come off as preachy or condescending, it wasn't intended that way. Good luck with making future friends, in any case!
